small.title: Why a small map can be flat
small.mini: On a sphere, the circle at distance d from a point is 2πR sin(d/R) long, not 2πd. The best flat map is off by c²/6 with c = d/R: a millionth for a town, 0.4 % for a kingdom, 1 % only 1,560 km from the centre.
small.text: The oldest surviving map of the world, a Babylonian clay tablet, is a disc around Babylon [2], and for local maps a plane was the right model. Draw the best possible flat map of a region: every distance and direction from its centre exact. On a sphere of radius R, the circle at ground distance d from the centre is 2πR sin(d/R) long; the map draws it 2πd long, a stretch of c/sin c ≈ 1 + c²/6 with c = d/R [1]. That is under a millionth for a town, 0.004 % for a county, 0.4 % for a kingdom 1,000 km across, and 1 % only 1,560 km from the centre. Errors grow as the square of the map's size, which is why flat maps served for millennia and fail for the whole world.
small.verdict: Does not separate the models at small scale, and says so: a flat map of a few hundred kilometres is as good as a globe. The test is whether one flat map can hold the whole world.
small.labels: The circle on the sphere and on paper|Error of the best flat map, by region size
erat.title: Eratosthenes sizes the Earth with a shadow
erat.mini: At noon on the solstice the Sun was overhead at Syene and 1/50 of a circle from the vertical at Alexandria, 5,000 stadia north. So the Earth is 50 × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia around.
erat.text: Around 240 BCE Eratosthenes compared two places on the same meridian [1]. At Syene the noon Sun at the summer solstice stood overhead; at Alexandria, 5,000 stadia to the north, a gnomon's shadow showed it 1/50 of a full circle, 7.2°, from the vertical. Sunbeams are parallel, so the same 7.2° is the angle between the two places at the Earth's centre, and the circumference is 360°/7.2° × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia. The length of his stadion is uncertain, so is the result in kilometres; the method, an angle and a distance, is the one every later measurement of the Earth repeats.
erat.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth: two places whose noon shadows differ by an angle that does not grow in proportion to the distance between them along the meridian.
ptolemy.title: Ptolemy's world, recomputed from his own coordinates
ptolemy.mini: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 CE) gives 6,372 places by latitude and longitude and a conic projection true on every meridian and on 36° and 63°. Recomputed, his latitudes are close; his longitudes run 1.40 times too fast: 252,000 / 180,000 stadia.
ptolemy.text: Ptolemy's Geography, around 150 CE, lists places by latitude and longitude, angles on a sphere, and explains how to draw them on a plane [1]. His first projection bends the parallels into concentric arcs and runs the meridians straight to a point above the pole, so that every meridian and the parallels of Rhodes (36°) and Thule (63°) keep their true length, cos φ of the equator: an equidistant conic, a cone set on a globe [4]. Here the 6,372 coordinates of his catalogue [2] are drawn through that projection inside his frame, 63° N to 16°25′ S over 180° of longitude; underneath, the modern coastlines through the same projection. For 56 towns whose site is known, a line joins where he puts them to where they are: latitudes agree within a couple of degrees, but longitudes grow 1.40 times too fast eastward, almost exactly Eratosthenes' 252,000 stadia over the 180,000 Ptolemy adopted. Beside it, the oldest surviving map drawn from his lists, a Byzantine manuscript of about 1300, on the same projection [3]. The method was a globe's; the error was in the size of the globe.
ptolemy.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth: parallels whose measured lengths do not shrink as cos φ toward the north.
mercator.title: Mercator's map: straight headings, wrong sizes
mercator.mini: Mercator (1569) drew meridians parallel and stretched north–south as much as east–west, sec φ, so shapes and angles stay true and a straight line is a constant compass heading. Sizes are not: ×10.5 in area at 72° N.
mercator.text: A navigator wants a straight line on the chart to be one compass heading. Gerardus Mercator's world map of 1569 draws the meridians parallel, which widens each parallel by sec φ, and widens the north–south direction by the same factor at every latitude, so that angles and small shapes stay true [1]. Edward Wright computed the spacing in 1599 by adding up sec φ: y = R ln tan(π/4 + φ/2) [1][2]. Equal circles of the globe stay round and swell toward the poles; at 72° N areas are drawn 10.5 times too large. The straight line from Frankfurt to San Francisco is a constant heading of 10,540 km; the great circle, the shortest route that airliners fly, is 9,150 km and arcs toward the pole on this map.
mercator.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth drawn as this rectangle: straight lines on it being the shortest routes. Measured routes follow the great circles instead.
tissot.title: No flat map keeps everything
tissot.mini: Gauss (1827): a sphere's curvature 1/R² can be measured from lengths alone, and a plane's is 0, so no map keeps every length. Tissot's circles show what each projection gives up: shapes, areas or distances.
tissot.text: Carl Friedrich Gauss proved in 1827 that the curvature of a surface can be measured from inside it, from lengths alone, and that no bending without stretching changes it [1]. A plane has zero curvature and a sphere 1/R²: no map of any part of a sphere keeps every length. Nicolas Auguste Tissot showed in 1881 how to see the cost: small equal circles on the globe become ellipses on the map, with semi-axes h along the meridian and k along the parallel [2]. A conformal map keeps h = k (Mercator), an equal-area map keeps hk = 1 (Lambert's cylinder of 1772, the sinusoidal), the azimuthal equidistant keeps h = 1 along lines from its centre [3]. The same circles, 1,560 km across on the ground, are drawn on six maps.
tissot.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth: a world map on which equal measured circles all come out the same size and shape.
ae.title: The azimuthal equidistant map: true from one point
ae.mini: Put one place at the centre, draw every other at its true distance and direction from it. Distances from the centre are right; others are not: on the North-Pole map Sydney–Santiago is 25,680 km, against 11,350 km on the ground.
ae.text: The azimuthal equidistant projection puts one place at the centre and every other place at its true distance and true direction from it: ρ = R c, with c the angle at the Earth's centre, and the azimuth kept [1]. Mercator used it in 1569 for his inset of the Arctic; it is the map radio amateurs centre on their station. Along each line from the centre the scale is exactly 1; across them it is c/sin c, 1.57 at 90° from the centre and without limit at the rim, which is a single point, the antipode, drawn as a circle. With the centre at the North Pole, the straight line from Sydney to Santiago measures 25,680 km on the map; the great-circle distance is 11,350 km, the distance flown.
ae.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth: one centre for which every measured distance between cities, not only those from the centre, matches the map's straight lines.
centres.title: One globe, a different flat map for every centre
centres.mini: The same rule — true distance and direction from the centre — applied around the North Pole, Paris, Mecca, Cape Town, the South Pole, Sydney and Honolulu gives seven different flat maps, each correct from its own centre.
centres.text: The azimuthal equidistant projection can be centred anywhere [1]. The centre here travels along great circles from the North Pole to Paris, Mecca, Cape Town, the South Pole, Sydney and Honolulu, and the map is redrawn at every step from the same coastlines with the same rule: each place at its true distance and direction from the centre. Every one of these maps is as correct as the North-Pole map used to depict a flat Earth, and every one is wrong away from its centre; the rim is always the single point opposite the centre. Nothing in the rule singles out the North Pole: it is a choice, a free parameter of any flat model built on this map.
centres.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth: one particular centre whose map, alone among them, matches measured distances between all pairs of places.
gleason.title: The flat-earth map is a globe map
gleason.mini: Gleason's 1892 'New Standard Map of the World' and the 1946 UN emblem are both azimuthal equidistant projections centred on the North Pole. Parallels are drawn (π/2 − φ)/cos φ too long: ×2.6 at Sydney's latitude.
gleason.text: In 1892 Alexander Gleason of Buffalo published a 'New Standard Map of the World' on a north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection, patented in 1893 as a time chart; he took it to support his belief that the round Earth was false [1]. The United Nations emblem, adopted in 1946, is the same projection cut at 60° S [2]. Its grid is computed from latitudes and longitudes on a globe: each parallel is a circle whose radius is its true distance from the pole, so it is drawn 2πR(π/2 − φ) long instead of 2πR cos φ [3]. East–west distances come out 1.08 times too long at London's latitude, 1.57 at the equator, 2.61 at Sydney's, and without limit toward the rim; equal circles of the globe turn into ever longer ellipses southward. Distances from the North Pole, and along meridians, are exact.
gleason.verdict: Would favour a flat Earth: measured east–west distances in the south, Sydney–Santiago or Johannesburg–Perth, matching this map's straight lines rather than the globe's great circles.
gleason.labels: Gleason's polar map, equal circles of the globe|East–west stretch against latitude
utm.title: Today's maps are flat again, in 6° strips
utm.mini: UTM cuts the globe into 60 zones 6° wide, each mapped flat. The scale is 0.9996 on the central meridian, 1 about 180 km away, 1.001 at the zone's edge: flat works, in small pieces, for the same reason as ever.
utm.text: The Universal Transverse Mercator grid, used by surveyors, armies and phone maps, cuts the globe into sixty zones 6° of longitude wide, from 80° S to 84° N, and maps each zone on its own cylinder touching the globe along the zone's central meridian [1]. Inside a zone the ground is treated as a plane. The scale is set to 0.9996 on the central meridian so that it is exactly 1 about 180 km either side and 1.001 at the zone's edge, 334 km away at the equator: k ≈ k₀(1 + x²/2R²). The error grows as the square of the distance, like any flat map of a small region, and that is why the zones stop at 6°.
utm.verdict: Does not separate the models within one zone; the joins between zones, which a single plane would not need, are where the sphere shows.
